title: A new poll shows what voters are thinking 2 weeks out from Election Day
description:
Midterm election day is just over two weeks away. What are some numbers on the mind of voters?   

    
        
          Transcript
body:
Midterm election day is just over two weeks away. What are some numbers on the mind of voters?   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  We begin this hour with some numbers. Fifteen - that is the number of days until Election Day. Two hundred eighteen to 214 - that is the current advantage Republicans hold in the House of Representatives. And 46 - that is how many House seats the Cook Political Report calls competitive in the midterm.JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:  Four is how many seats Democrats need to net to win back the Senate. Here are some other figures on the minds of voters. Thirty-nine percent is the number of Americans who approve of President Trump's job performance. That's according to the latest NPR/ PBS and Marist poll. That's down from 44% when he started his second term.DETROW: And if you're seeking some scale, how about $10 billion? That is what has been spent on the 2026 elections as of last week, and that is just the money spent on ads - TV, digital radio - not including pizza and doughnuts for the field offices.SUMMERS: Two dollars and 98 cents is a much smaller sum. That was the average price of a gallon of gas nearly eight months ago, according to AAA's price tracker. Today, a fill-up will cost a lot more. The average price of regular gas is up to $4.30 a gallon.DETROW: And what's something that a number of Americans agree about this election year? Data centers - people don't like them. In our poll, 58% of voters say the construction of data centers by tech companies will have a negative impact on the country.SUMMERS: And if this all feels like just a whole lot of numbers, well, we're going to leave you with one more. The next presidential election date is 750 days away.

title: Judge chastises Trump administration plan to push ahead overhaul of DC golf course
description: Golfers make their way around the course
body:
Golfers make their way around the course at East Potomac Golf Links on October. The National Park Service confirmed in a filing had marked over 500 trees for removal as the Trump Administration mulls over a renovation for the golf course.
                
                    Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images
    

   
   In a tense hearing on Monday, federal Judge Ana C. Reyes sharply rebuked administration lawyers over President Trump's apparent intent to defy the court and proceed with a major renovation of the historic East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C. Only days before, the judge had temporarily blocked the government from moving forward with the project.   During the hearing, which ended without a decision, Reyes chastised the government attorneys, who had previously told the court that renovating the links was still in its conceptual stage. So when Trump posted his detailed plans for a new golf course on Sunday, Reyes wanted to know who was responsible for misleading the court.   
   "Do I believe the president of the United States or do I believe you?" she asked.   During the hearing, Reyes frequently exhibited frustration and annoyance. "I have, on the one hand, the president of the United States saying to the American public three times now, I think, in the last two days, there is a final plan to redesign the golf course," she said. "Then I have you all telling me and, you know, witnesses saying what they're saying, that there's no final plan. Which is it?"   Trump has said that he wants to turn the three existing courses at the East Potomac Golf Links into a single, "championship-style golf course." But in February, a D.C. preservation group and two individuals challenged the U.S. Department of Interior and the National Park Service over the planned renovations, arguing that the renovated course would inflate tee-time costs for a facility that was originally intended to be "open to all people."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The East Potomac Park Golf Course covers a peninsula between the Potomac River and the Washington Channel.
                
                    Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP
    

   
   In May, the judge ordered the administration to give notice of any substantial construction work on the course, including the removal of more than 10 trees. Despite the order, late on Friday, Oct. 9 — just before a holiday weekend — government officials notified the court that it planned to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases.   
   Bulldozers began taking down hundreds of trees the next day. During a three-hour emergency hearing last week, Reyes called the government lawyers out for not giving enough prior notice for the tree removal. She did not believe the argument that the tree felling was part of routine maintenance, saying she was "beyond disappointed" by the action and ordered a 24-hour halt.   Judge: "Every single benefit of the doubt"   "I do not know how I could have made it any plainer that I did not want what was to happen, to happen," she said, adding: "I have given the government every single benefit of the doubt that it would not do precisely what it has done."   On Friday, the White House filed a motion requesting that Reyes remove herself from the case, accusing her of bias. The judge declined to step aside.   Ahead of the hearing on Monday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Reyes was a "crazed lunatic" and said that renovation work did not need court approval. "Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY!" he said. The president's post appears to contradict a response filed by Department of Justice lawyers the previous day indicating that "the plan is not final because the Park Service has not completed its review."   Trump has described the golf course as "old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect." The prospect of a complete renovation has alarmed residents who are concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.   A protected landmark   The century-old golf links were also one of the first public courses to be desegregated. "This is not just some putt-putt course," Reyes told the attorneys, who appeared in court on Monday. The park holds "a deep amount of meaning for the people of the district, and is protected as a historic landmark."   
   The White House has said that it is simply carrying out a 2019 preservation plan, but plaintiffs seeking to block the changes have said that Trump's stated desire to redevelop the course goes well beyond that. Among other things, the 2019 plan recommends removing invasive vegetation that doesn't contribute to the historic landscape, but not healthy, native species.   The golf course is one of several instances in which the president has sought to circumvent the courts in order to exert his power and to place his own stamp on Washington, D.C. He has also threatened to tear down the Kennedy Center and is seeking to build a 250-foot arch near the National Mall.

title: The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races
description: Election workers process ballots for the
body:
Election workers process ballots for the California state primary at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on June 5. California's relatively slow vote count has put "a big target on its back," one expert told NPR.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   Stephen Richer no longer runs elections in the fourth-largest county in the country.   But for the rest of his life, he'll remember the feeling when polls closed on an election night.   More than a million ballots staring at him and his staff. Every moment that passes without them fully counted means another conspiracy theory sprouting online.   "Those days, those were hell for me," said Richer, a Republican who served as the clerk and recorder for Arizona's Maricopa County. "You'd have a limited number of workers, and you'd have a limited amount of space, and you'd be doing everything that you possibly could. … And yet you have everyone blowing up your phone, everyone saying that you're incompetent or corrupt or worse."   
   This midterm year, election officials in competitive congressional districts will face that same pressure.   But they will also face a hard reality: that those races might not be called until days after Election Day.   Here's an FAQ on why that is, and what it could mean this year.   Why do we know the results immediately in some places, and in others it takes days or weeks?   It comes down to the margin of victory.   Which sounds strange, since who wins an election and by how much shouldn't impact how long it takes election officials to count ballots.   But the reality is what most Americans think of as "election results" — the winners announced on election nights across TV networks and social media — are not the result of all ballots being counted, but rather, races being called by news organizations that determine the winners based on a state or district's demographics and initial returns. (NPR relies on The Associated Press for its race calls.)   Those determinations come a lot faster when races aren't close.   "Margins matter," said Richer, who noted that in recent elections, there has been a lot less scrutiny on Utah than there has been on his home state of Arizona, or certain contests in California, despite the states counting votes at similar speeds.   
   "In Utah you can call all the races very quickly because the Republicans there have high margins," Richer said.   That gives the illusion of elections there being complete, but no state is done counting ballots on election night, even if it seems that way because notable races are called early.   
   So you're saying the timing of results isn't at all tied to vote-counting speed?   Not exactly.   The closer the race, the more election analysts need to see before they can make a call. So the faster states count ballots, the faster those determinations can be made.   This is why the longest wait times every election usually come from places that have competitive races and which also count slowly.   Like, California?   Exactly. California has become the poster child for long results times because of both those factors: a bevy of competitive congressional districts, which help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House, and a vote count that's been among the slowest in the nation.   Add in that President Trump, the most prominent purveyor of election misinformation in the country, has long targeted the liberal California, and experts see a perfect storm for false voting narratives.   "It's progressive, it likes mail ballots, it gets [postmarked] mail ballots after Election Day," Richer said. "It just all adds up to a fairly incendiary situation."   Charles Stewart, an elections expert at MIT, put it more simply.   "California just has a big target on its back," said Stewart.   California's slow vote counting caused a lot of conspiracy theorizing during the state's June primary. Is this fall going to be a rerun?   Kim Alexander is cautiously optimistic that won't be the case.   She runs the California Voter Foundation, which has been advocating for ways to speed up California's vote tally without giving up the state's generous voting access policies, like mailing every active registered voter a ballot.   
   "We have all these amazing rights and opportunities that we give to our voters, and the price we're paying is a longer vote count," Alexander told NPR. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be this long."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                An election worker processes ballots for the California state primary at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on June 5.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   The single biggest cause for California's slow count comes from a phenomenon Alexander calls "the pig in the python" problem: a logjam of millions of vote-by-mail ballots getting returned on Election Day that need to be processed.   Those ballots take longer to count than in-person votes, as officials need to deal with envelopes and verify signatures to make sure mail ballots are cast by the people they're supposed to be cast by.   Some counties see up to 50% of their vote-by-mail ballots turned in on Election Day, Alexander said, which means processing work doesn't even begin until later in the week.   "I can't tell you how many people who are informed and engaged and … when I tell them that the cause for the long vote count is voters holding on to their ballots to Election Day and turning them in, they look at me and they're like, 'That's what I do,'" Alexander said. "And I'm like, 'I know! You're part of the problem!'"   The state allocated $40 million to speeding up its counting this year, and part of that money is going to voter education.   Alexander is optimistic that once voters learn they can play a role in speeding up the process by voting earlier, or by utilizing other voting methods that allow for quicker counting, they will respond.   "California has been beaten up by this president for over a decade over our election process, and it's gotten pretty worrisome," Alexander said. "I think that California voters, if they feel they can do something to respond to that, many will take action."   
   To that point, research conducted earlier this year found that when voters in California's San Joaquin County received postcards urging them to vote earlier, they were more likely to meet the recommended deadline that allowed for election-night counting.   
   Alexander noted one more change that could mean less spotlight on California this year: fewer competitive House districts.   Ahead of the 2022 elections, the state had nine districts that the Cook Political Report considered competitive. But this year, in part because voters approved a mid-cycle gerrymander to respond to gerrymanders in Republican-controlled states, the state has just three.   That makes it less likely the entire country will be waiting on California to know who controls the House.   OK, anywhere else we should be watching when it comes to results speed?   Using the formula discussed earlier (competitive races + slow vote counting), it's impossible not to look at Alaska.   According to data from the MIT Election Lab, Alaska was the last state in 2024 to reach 95% of its ballots counted.   Election Day was Nov. 5 that year, but the state's lone House race — which Republican Nicholas Begich won by fewer than 10,000 votes — wasn't called by the AP until Nov. 20.   This year, polling shows a tight Alaska Senate race. That means, if results fall a certain way in other states, the entire country could be waiting weeks to know which party will control the U.S. Senate next year.

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                People vote in Norwalk, Calif., during early voting in California's primary election on June 1, 2026. The Department of Justice has charged 28 green card holders in the state for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections, in an escalation of a feud with California officials over the state's voting system.
                
                    Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 The DOJ wants California to segregate ballots of those on its list and to delay counting them until investigations are complete. Election law experts doubt the DOJ will succeed, given its past attempts to change state voting processes, Miles Parks tells Up First. He adds that it would be surprising to see a shift just two weeks before the election with ballots already distributed. Research shows that in many cases, when legal permanent residents register to vote, it is due to a misunderstanding of the rules. Experts tell Parks they are concerned that federal law enforcement might use accusations to confiscate ballots during counting, but many local voting officials are preparing by keeping county attorneys on speed dial.   
   Democrats and Republicans are deciding which races to prioritize with Election Day just two weeks away. President Trump is campaigning in key perennial purple states like Georgia, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Florida this week.   🎧 Trump's rally in Kansas and trip to North Carolina aren't where the leader of the Republican Party's attention should be, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and many Republican groups have ceased ad spending in North Carolina, viewing the Senate race as a lost cause. Republicans are prioritizing efforts to save their Senate majority over saving the House majority, while Democrats are capitalizing on opportunities in conservative areas, Fowler says. In Georgia, with a million voters already casting ballots, Fowler says he sees an increase in Black voter turnout in the state and across the South.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns about the app's risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content. Previously unreported court records show employees' frustration with leadership's response to these issues. Depositions filed in March 2026 provide new insights into TikTok's child safety measures since its surge in popularity in 2018. Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. They also identified loopholes that allowed users under 18 to bypass age restrictions and block parental oversight of their app activity. The records show that TikTok avoided conducting age surveys, fearing it would have to share results with the Federal Trade Commission.   
   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Andee Tagle/NPR
    

   
   Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.   🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects. Some good medications to have include ibuprofen or naproxen, which can relieve headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation and Acetaminophen, which can lower body temperature.🤒 Honey acts as an anti-inflammatory and soothes the throat, making it useful for young children who can't take cough medicine. But don't give it to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.🤒 A thermometer is a must-have for checking your temperature. For children 3 and under, a rectal option is preferred.🤒 A saline spray or rinse for your nose can help keep the mucous membranes moist and help relieve symptoms by loosening thick mucus during a cold.   For more advice on how to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                American Girl dolls of all eras on display at the store, September 24, 2026, New York, New York.
                
                    Lanna Apisukh for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Lanna Apisukh for NPR
    

   
   Pleasant Rowland launched Pleasant Company in 1986 with three dolls — Samantha, Molly and Kirsten — creating an empire known as American Girl. To celebrate its 40th anniversary, author Fiona Davis was asked to write a historical fiction book for adults titled Samantha: The Next Chapter, featuring Samantha Parkington, who has turned 25. The story picks up after Samantha's last book, in which she attended a suffragist rally with her aunt Cornelia. The book is set 15 years later, in 1920, just after the ratification of the 19th Amendment. Samantha learns that her grandmother's inheritance has been stolen, forcing her to transition from socialite to shopgirl overnight. NPR's Samantha Balaban visited the American Girl store in New York with her own Samantha doll to explore the character's evolution over the years, drawing on insights from its staff and Davis. Check out photos from the visit and read more about the history of American Girl dolls.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause.
                
                    BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images
    

   
   The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its menopause treatment guidelines for the first time since 2014. The group now recommends using hormone replacement therapy along with some other treatments to alleviate symptoms.A wedding day can be one of the costliest days in a couple's life. Some are opting to save money by choosing grocery-store cakes over specialty bakers' cakes.Vegemite is such an iconic breakfast spread in Australia that a convicted killer is suing the state of Victoria for the right to eat it in prison. The state has banned Vegemite because it could potentially be used to brew alcohol and throw off dogs.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate
description: People vote in Norwalk, Calif., during e
body:
People vote in Norwalk, Calif., during early voting in California's primary election on June 1, 2026. The Department of Justice has charged 28 green card holders in the state for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections, in an escalation of a feud with California officials over the state's voting system.
                
                    Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The Justice Department announced on Monday it was charging 28 noncitizens with election crimes in California, signaling a further escalation over the state's voting system that looks like it will continue through Election Day and beyond.   The DOJ also filed an emergency request in federal court to stop California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls whom the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." The state has asked for specific information on how the federal government came to its conclusions, but has not received it.   "This Department of Justice will not look the other way while noncitizens vote in federal elections," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said at a press conference on Monday announcing the election crime charges. "Unfortunately the same can't be said for California and L.A. County."   
   Noncitizen voting has never been found to be a widespread problem in American elections, but the Trump administration is devoting significant resources to uncovering the ineligible voting that does occur. The DOJ has been announcing handfuls of new charges almost every day as early voting gets underway in many states.   The Justice Department's latest request in federal court is a continuation of a saga that began this summer with President Trump's primetime speech on election integrity. It took a major turn last week with the delivery of a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them. Local and state officials declined to do so, and the federal government sued.   McCotter escalated the dispute further on Friday by warning California officials in a letter that they could be criminally prosecuted for knowingly processing ballots "cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens." President Trump wrote on Truth Social that evening: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"   Taken together, the threats have local officials and election experts worried that the adversarial posture of the Justice Department towards California portends more actions to come aimed at delegitimizing results in this fall's midterms.   
   "There's a few things to be worried about," said Rick Hasen, an election law expert who runs UCLA's Safeguarding Democracy Project. "One is the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters. The other is the risk that it further undermines voter confidence in the electoral process by making it seem like [noncitizen voting] is a major problem when it is not. And the third risk is that this is going to be used as some sort of pretext to try to seize ballots or interfere after the election is over."   Dana Lewis, the Republican county recorder for Pinal County, Ariz., said local officials nationwide are watching and communicating about what's happening in California, the same way they did when the FBI raided an elections office in Fulton County, Ga. in January.   If those officials are administering a race this fall that is close or contested, they feel they could be next, she said.   "When this impacts another jurisdiction, you automatically have to feel that," Lewis said. "If it's happening in Georgia, if it's happening in Colorado or California, we're all watching."   New criminal charges against noncitizens in California   All 28 people charged in California on Monday are green-card holders, and all appeared on the list of 20,000 names the DOJ gave California officials last week, according to DOJ officials.   A number of them do not appear to have actually voted, and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago. Many are accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications, which ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship.   
   Previous research has shown that when noncitizen voting and registration occurs, it is also often the result of bureaucratic error and not intentional fraud. New Jersey revealed this summer that a software glitch at the DMV registered more than 6,000 people to vote even though they had indicated they were noncitizens.   Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for California's Central District, downplayed that possibility on Monday, however.   "It's not something that just happens to you," Essayli said. "They either attested to it when they got a driver's license, or they went out of their way to file a voter registration form, and they swore under oath that they were a citizen."   
   In the past seven weeks, the Justice Department has charged 113 noncitizens across 20 states with voting and registration crimes, officials said at Monday's press conference.   UCLA's Hasen said the charges seem to be meant to make noncitizen voting "look like a bigger issue than it is."   "Given that there's over 20 million registered voters in California, this is quite a small number of allegations," Hasen said. "And we don't know how many of these allegations will even pan out. And so even if all of these were in fact people who were illegally voting, it's a drop in the bucket compared to the number of voters in California."   
   Recent polling suggests a sizable portion of the American public thinks immigration enforcement will be present at voting locations this fall, despite federal law banning armed federal agents from the polls. Non-white voters are more likely than white voters to say they fear voting could put them at risk of being questioned by immigration authorities despite being citizens.   In an interview earlier this fall with NPR, Los Angeles County's top voting official, Dean Logan, alluded to those worries.   "Given everything leading up to this election, what we're trying to remind voters is the best way to secure the election is through your participation," Logan told NPR. "Don't be distracted by the litigation. Don't be distracted by the mis- and disinformation. If you have questions, let us know, let us answer them. But don't let this keep you from voting," he said.   "Because if you're not voting, none of the rest matters, right?"   An unprecedented demand by DOJ   The Justice Department's request that a federal judge block California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots from the list of 20,000 "likely noncitizens" it gave state officials last week is unprecedented and an especially unusual request given that voting is already underway.   
   California officials have argued that complying with the Department's demand to set the ballots aside would be unlawful and noted the DOJ has not confirmed that the voters on the list are noncitizens.   "The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote to the DOJ's McCotter on Oct. 13.   "Withholding ballots from some duly registered voters and segregating and refusing to tabulate voted ballots submitted by others, is an unprecedented suspension — and even denial — of voting rights," she wrote.   Los Angeles County's assistant county counsel, Peter Bollinger, wrote to McCotter on Oct. 15: "we are not authorized to, or are prohibited from, taking the actions requested in your letter under both federal and state law. The actions described would disenfranchise those in question without due process." The same letter noted the list of names from the DOJ included voters from outside Los Angeles County, whom the office does not maintain any records on.   Both letters cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law that bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters from state voter rolls during the 90 days before an election. The law is supposed to prevent mistakes that could erroneously purge eligible voters right before an election without giving voters time to correct errors.   
   There are also questions about the methodology the Trump administration used to come up with its tally of 20,000 likely noncitizens and its accuracy. A July letter to California from the Department of Homeland Security alleged the state had a potential of 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls.   In Monday's press briefing, McCotter said the 20,000 figure represented the people the Justice Department had the most confidence were noncitizens after DHS cross-referenced various government databases and other records with identifying information.   McCotter and other DOJ officials blamed California for not handing over its entire voter roll — including partial Social Security Numbers and driver's license numbers — which they said could help shed more light on the citizenship status of these voters. So far 26 federal judges have dismissed DOJ demands for that data across the country.   
   In the Justice Department's Monday filing for a restraining order preventing California from counting ballots from the 20,000 individuals, the DOJ wrote: "Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm may be impossible to remedy. The urgency is heightened because of the fundamental right to vote and to have one's lawful vote counted without dilution."   A half dozen voting and civil rights organizations filed to intervene in the case last week to argue the DOJ's demands are unlawful.   Election experts have said the DOJ's lawsuit against California seems more about sending a political message or teeing up future challenges than winning this case in court, given that the constitution gives states the authority to administer elections.   "I expect this lawsuit to go nowhere," UCLA's Hasen wrote last week.

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   The 2026 midterm elections are set to become the most expensive on record. More than $15 billion has been raised to influence the outcome and control of Congress.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Election workers process ballots for the California state primary at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on June 5. California's relatively slow vote count has put "a big target on its back," as one election expert told NPR.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Democratic nominees in House and Senate races are raking in incredible amounts of donations, even though the Democratic Party remains unpopular, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Republicans are also unpopular, largely due to issues like the war in Iran, gas prices and the economy. A few megadonors, such as Elon Musk, are donating money to super PACs to try to push voters to elect Republicans. In the 13 competitive races highlighted in the Cook Political Report, Republicans are being outraised by a 5-to-1 margin. Both parties are spending heavily, indicating that Democrats might have a chance to win in several locations. Currently, 75% of planned ad buys are in toss-up races or those leaning Republican.➡️ Some of the most competitive congressional races might not be called until days after Election Day. Here's why.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   
   At least one person died and more than a dozen were injured in a major Ukrainian drone strike yesterday on Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital. The attack targeted strategic sites, including a key port oil terminal. Over the weekend, Russian missile strikes in Ukraine killed at least 11 people. This conflict continues as President Trump says that relieving pressure on Russia is the best way to end the war.   🎧 The recent attack on Saint Petersburg appears to mark the largest one on the city since Russia's 2022 invasion, NPR's Charles Maynes tells Up First. While it's unclear how many drones struck the city, Russia's Defense Ministry reported intercepting 1,000 drones across various regions that night. Trump seems to be working to protect Russian oil facilities after cutting a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel. The move was aimed at lowering gas prices for U.S. voters before the midterm elections. Trump has called previous Ukrainian strikes a "disgrace," even as Russia continues to strike Ukraine, Maynes says. He adds that the president blames President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacks that allegedly raise U.S. fuel prices, despite economists attributing the price increase mainly to Trump's war in Iran.   French President Emmanuel Macron denounced violence over the weekend that he says has overshadowed largely peaceful protests across the country. The unrest began as a student protest for better conditions and has expanded to include public-sector workers protesting high energy prices, the rising cost of living and social inequality. The Interior Ministry reported about 2,300 arrests and nearly 1,000 injured police officers.   
   🎧 NPR's Eleanor Beardsley, who was in the streets of Paris yesterday, witnessed burned bikes, shattered glass and graffiti on looted stores saying things like "tax the rich." She spoke with 23-year-old Sarah Berlia, who says she believes these actions come from a frustrated generation facing dwindling rights and opportunities. Beardsley says the protest culture in France often attracts "troublemakers," but the scale of current events is massive. The protests have had political implications, as France is six months away from a presidential election. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has joined the protesters, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, has condemned the violence and the government.   Living better   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Tony Stepanow, from Finland, attends a sauna during the International Sauna Congress 2026 in Oslo, Norway, Sept. 25, 2026.
                
                    Siv Dolmen for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Siv Dolmen for NPR
    

   
   Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.   Saunas are gaining renewed attention in the wellness world for their potential to improve mental health. This trend reflects the growing interest in the broader wellness movement and social connection, especially post-pandemic. While scientists understand how saunas affect the cardiovascular system, they are just beginning to explore their impact on mental health. Here's what they know so far.   🥵 When our skin detects heat, it sends signals to a primitive brain area that prompts our body to cool down. This pathway also influences mood and pleasure, which is associated with depression.🥵 Heat triggers an anti-inflammatory response similar to the effects of exercise, which is known to help with depression and other mental health issues.🥵 Heating people up can act like a "thermoregulatory workout," helping their bodies cool down more efficiently over time.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jennifer Teresa Villanueva's aunts, cousins, grandmother and uncle gather around the dining table for an afternoon brunch at home in Chicago in 2018.
                
                    Jennifer Teresa Villanueva
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jennifer Teresa Villanueva
    

   
   Artist Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has captured her family's everyday life through her lens for eight years, revealing moments of love, care and sacrifice within their Chicago home. The personal project took root in 2018, sparked by her grandmother's hospitalization. It started as a way to better understand her grandmother's daily routines, and soon it blossomed into a heartfelt exploration of the immigrant experience. "I am interested in what happens when the camera enters a home where everyone already knows one another," Villanueva told NPR. "There is no distance between photographer and subject. I am photographing the people who raised me, and I am also photographing the home that raised me." See photos from the project and read more about Villanueva's work.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Noah Adams adjusts his headphones in the National Public Radio studio in Washington Feb.16, 1987.
                
                    Charles Tasnadi/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Charles Tasnadi/AP
    

   
   Noah Adams, a writer and broadcaster who hosted All Things Considered for 18 years, has died. He was 84 years old.Trump announced over the weekend that he plans to close and renovate the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C. The golf course is already at the center of a legal battle.An Air Force service member died Saturday after a rappelling accident during a pregame ceremony at the Alamodome ahead of the University of Texas at San Antonio's football game against Navy. (via Texas Public Radio)   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., on Trump waiving sanctions on Russia
description: NPR's Leila Fadel asks Democratic Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia  about President Trump's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia.
body:
NPR's Leila Fadel asks Democratic Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia  about President Trump's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    LEILA FADEL, HOST:  Let's get a view from Capitol Hill on President Trump's decision to waive new Russia sanctions. Democratic Representative Don Beyer of Virginia is on the line. Congressman, good morning and welcome back to the program.DON BEYER: Thank you, Leila, very much.FADEL: So you've called President Trump's move a, quote, "surrender to Putin." What makes it a surrender, in your view?BEYER: Well, back to the historic mistake that Zelenskyy has just mentioned. So far, it's been like Munich in 1938, where Trump has just done his best to appease Putin again and again. But now we unfortunately passed this Lindsey Graham bill to put sanctions on Russia and give Trump basically unlimited tariff authority against anybody who wanted. And the first thing he'd done is waive those sanctions on Russia.FADEL: Well, let me ask you about that because in the executive order, the president also says that the sanctions law on Russia and Iran, which is named for Lindsey Graham, it's supposed to cut off revenue for Russia's war in Ukraine, but actually gives him the power to waive the sanctions. That's right?BEYER: It does, which was - we pointed out at the time this is a bad bill. But not only did he waive the sanctions, but he also announced, you know, a $4 billion purchase of diesel fuel, which was clearly illegal with the '19 - or 2022 law that said we can't buy any of that oil from Russia.FADEL: In your statement, you call on Congress to fix this flawed law. What would that look like?BEYER: Well, just right away, before we passed the Lindsey Graham bill, the House had already passed a bill that placed the sanctions on Russia, did not give Trump the ability to waive them, and also didn't give him this new tariff authority. We need to bring that bill back right away.FADEL: Now, in a Truth Social post on Sunday, President Trump justified his decision by saying he wants to avoid driving Russia away from the bargaining table. Does relaxing sanctions on Russia make it easier for the U.S. to negotiate peace between Russia and Ukraine?BEYER: That strategy certainly hasn't worked for the last 4 1/2 years. Also Trump has gone after Zelenskyy again and again, pointing out that he doesn't want peace. The news that I read says Zelenskyy has said again he will do anything he can to stop attacking Russia as long as Russia stops attacking them.FADEL: Now, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Saturday that waiving sanctions is about the global economy. Let's just listen to what he said.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARCO RUBIO: The problem is these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries - India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy.FADEL: Congressman, does this make sense to you?BEYER: That's laughable. This is the same man, the same president, who's imposed, for example, 50% tariffs on India at one time, 39% against Switzerland. He's imposed tariffs all over the world for the flimsiest of reasons. The notion that he's concerned about tariffs right now doesn't make any sense.FADEL: Now, the other thing that the president has said, he blames not his war on Iran, but Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel fuel targets for driving up oil prices. As a member of the House Ways and Means Trade Subcommittee, how do you see it?BEYER: Well, given that we've had sanctions against Russia for the last number of years on buying oil, it makes no sense at all to say that the Russia-Ukraine war was driving up prices. We look back before he attacked Iran, and gas prices were down in the low $2 - diesel prices were 4. It's the war in Iran that has given us the highest diesel prices in the history of the country.FADEL: Could a pause on sanctions provide relief for American consumers?BEYER: Every economist I've seen, specialists in fossil fuels, say even with the $4 billion of diesel fuel, it wouldn't make but a penny or two difference on diesel prices.FADEL: What would you want to see - go ahead.BEYER: It wouldn't do it.FADEL: What would you want to see the president do in this moment?BEYER: Stand with Ukraine, with the rest of our allies in Europe, with democracies around the world, and stand up to, you know, the first major invasion in Europe since World War II.FADEL: How are your Republican colleagues reacting to his decision?BEYER: It's mixed, but the ones that I respect most have been horrified. This is not what they intended when they passed the Lindsey Graham bill. And I think almost every Democrat and most Republicans want us to back Ukraine strongly.FADEL: Neither Ukraine nor Russia has adhered to what Trump announced as a, quote, "energy ceasefire," refraining from striking at energy facilities. Could this sanctions waiver improve the chances for such a deal? Would it make it worse?BEYER: That's a perfect world, but I think it will make it worse. By the way, he announced that ceasefire without talking to either Russia or Ukraine. Both were surprised by his announcement.FADEL: Don Beyer is a Democratic member of Congress from Virginia. Thank you so much for your time, Congressman.BEYER: Thank you, Leila.FADEL: And we'll note that we asked a number of Republican lawmakers if they'd like to join us this morning. Those invitations remain open.

title: Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigns in GOP stronghold
description: Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is campaigning in the GOP stronghold of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, an area that has
body:
Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is campaigning in the GOP stronghold of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, an area that hasn't voted for a Democrat in Congress in over a decade.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Back in the U.S., let's go to Michigan, where both of the Senate candidates have been focusing on urban areas with lots of voters, like Detroit and its suburbs. With about two weeks to go until Election Day, the Democrat in the race is also carrying his message into a Republican stronghold. Michigan Public Radio's Russ McNamara reports.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)ABDUL EL-SAYED: How are we doing, Marquette?RUSS MCNAMARA, BYLINE: Hundreds packed a rally on the campus of Northern Michigan University to hear Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's stump speech last week. It capped a whirlwind three-stop tour, covering a couple hundred miles across the state's rural and rugged Upper Peninsula. The goal for El-Sayed is to reach out to Yoopers, a nickname for people who live in the Upper Peninsula, or UP, and draw in support from conservatives. It's a tall order. Approximately 60% of them voted for Donald Trump two years ago. El-Sayed told reporters that he learned a lot from this campaign trip to the UP and a prior one in June.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)EL-SAYED: Yoopers are commonsense, thoughtful people, and they don't like paying more in gas than they need to, don't like paying more in groceries. And they don't like being taken advantage of by a billionaire from New York.MCNAMARA: Still, Yoopers have a healthy skepticism for outsiders, according to Republican state representative Karl Bohnak. He's well known here. Before entering politics, Karl Bohnak was a TV meteorologist for about 30 years. He's backing the Republican candidate in this toss-up race, former Congressman Mike Rogers.KARL BOHNAK: To be honest with you, I don't pay much attention to Abdul. I don't even really know what his message is. I think he meant something like Medicare for All. But the only question I would have is, who's going to pay for that?MCNAMARA: Healthcare is an issue in the Upper Peninsula, with many having to drive 100 miles or more to see a specialist. Data from Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services show that nearly 1 in 3 UP residents are enrolled in Medicare, with 7% without insurance altogether. Bart Stupak was the last Democrat to represent the UP in the U.S. House choosing not to run for reelection in 2010. He endorsed Representative Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary but believes El-Sayed's messaging can resonate with Yoopers.BART STUPAK: Just showing up helps him tremendously to try to connect with not just Democrats, but all the voters, even those Republicans who are disenchanted with the party right now.MCNAMARA: Trips across rural Michigan are one part of a broader strategy to reach Republicans for El-Sayed.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)EL-SAYED: We got to be willing to invite them to a decision they have yet to make.MCNAMARA: Speaking to a crowd in Escanaba, El-Sayed called on his supporters to connect with conservative family and friends to explain his key messages of Medicare for All and getting money out of politics.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)EL-SAYED: Reach out to them, OK? We have an opportunity to build our country, not just watch it get torn down.MCNAMARA: While El-Sayed attempts to bridge a partisan gap, there is some hesitancy among moderates within his own party. In an interview late last week with Michigan Public Radio, former Congressman Stupak says some of El-Sayed's positions give him pause.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)STUPAK: I would have voted by now, but I just want to see how this plays out a little bit more. Yeah, I'm a Democrat, but that doesn't mean I vote for every Democrat that shows up on a ticket.MCNAMARA: With razor-thin margins in this U.S. Senate race, rural conservatives would be a nice get for El-Sayed but mean little if he can't shore up his own base.For NPR News, I'm Russ McNamara in Marquette, Michigan.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Democrats — and Elon Musk — continue to dominate midterm campaign fundraising
description: Tesla, SpaceX and X CEO Elon Musk attend
body:
Tesla, SpaceX and X CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on Sept. 29
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   The 2026 midterms are on track to be the most expensive on record, driven by enthusiasm for Democratic candidates and massive contributions by Republican megadonors, especially Elon Musk.   More than $15 billion has been raised since the start of 2025, according to Federal Election Commission data, and half of that has been spent so far. Ad spending on House and Senate races has topped $4 billion, with hundreds of millions of dollars more planned for the final two weeks of the election, according to AdImpact data.   After winning the White House and a narrow majority in the House and Senate in 2024, Republicans now face an electorate that has soured on President Trump's agenda amid an unpopular war in Iran, high fuel costs and rising prices.   
   The Democratic Party as a national brand is unpopular, too. But a crop of Senate candidates in more conservative-leaning states like Iowa, Texas, Kansas and Ohio, and Democratic hopefuls in newly competitive House districts, have surged in polls and fundraising.   Despite Democrats' fundraising advantage at the candidate level, Republican outside groups — including a trio of super PACs tied to Trump's MAGA, Inc. — have outspent Democrats on the airwaves to try to paint that party as too extreme to control Congress.   Here are four takeaways from the latest campaign finance filings and what they say about the sprint to Election Day.   Democratic Senate dominance   One of the more surprising developments this election cycle is the number of U.S. Senate races that have become competitive, driven in part by Republicans being outraised by their opponents by sometimes wide margins.   From July to September, the Democratic or independent candidate outraised their Republican opponent in 27 of the 35 Senate races on the ballot, posting a nearly 5-to-1 advantage in the 13 most competitive races.   
   Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico's main campaign committee reported bringing in about $60 million in the third quarter, which the campaign says is a record for a Senate campaign in that period before the election.   That is also more than what any other Senate candidate has raised the entire cycle, except Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia.   It's not just the longtime expensive toss-up races like Ohio, Texas and Michigan, either.   In the last fundraising quarter, Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton raised nearly $10 million into his primary campaign committee, compared to just $800,000 for incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.   
   Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde Smith reported less than $700,000 in contributions, while both Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Jim Risch of Idaho disclosed just under half a million dollars in third quarter receipts. Their opponents reported roughly double the haul.   Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats and have sought to use their fundraising edge, along with Republican unpopularity, to target races in states where Trump won as much as 60% of the vote.   Dozens of House incumbents are outraised   Next year's Congress is already set to have a record number of departures, and that's before you account for a number of incumbents who could lose in November.   
   The anti-incumbency vibe present throughout the primaries has continued with fundraising, with 50 sitting House members being outraised in the last quarter — about 90% of them Republicans.   
   Of the 17 vulnerable lawmakers on the National Republican Congressional Committee's list of "NRCC Patriots," only one – Pennsylvania Republican Brian Fitzpatrick – reported raising more cash than his opponent. Only three of the 27 challengers who are part of the "MAGA Majority" program — were the top fundraisers in their districts, too.   
   On the Democratic side, the only vulnerable incumbent tagged as a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee "Frontliner" who was outraised last quarter was Nevada Rep. Dina Titus, while 40 of the 46 seats targeted as "Red to Blue" flips saw the Democratic candidate raise more money.   That includes deep-red districts in Arkansas, Kentucky and Nevada that have seen a surge in ad spending from Republicans trying to protect those seats.   
   There are seven longer-shot "Districts In Play" that saw Democrats raise more money, including KS-02, MI-01, NE-02 and OH-10, all of which are in states with competitive Senate races.   Several of the races expected to be the closest in November saw eye-popping fundraising totals from both candidates, like the more than $7 million combined raised last quarter in the NY-17 contest between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley.   Conley's $5.4 million Q3 haul is the largest of any House campaign, and more than all but one incumbent U.S. Senator raised in the same time frame.   Musk's money dominates Texas   Last week's campaign filings also reveal a fuller picture of Musk's outsize role in funding the Republican effort to keep Congress, especially the Texas Senate race.In recent weeks, Musk donated $158 million to the Republican Senate Leadership Fund, $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, $89 million to his America PAC and $10 million to the pro-Ken Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC.   The Senate Leadership Fund contribution was then used to solely fund the Texas PAC, which has already spent more than $148 million to boost Paxton and attack Talarico.   
   To put the donation in perspective, Musk's contributions to the Texas PAC is more than the Talarico and Paxton campaigns have raised combined throughout the entire campaign cycle. It's roughly the amount spent on advertising for all 470 congressional races in the first week of September. For every dollar raised by a Senate campaign in the past three months, Musk spent about 56 cents just in Texas.   Still, advertising rules that give candidates more favorable rates mean the Musk money bomb does not go as far, especially in the broader deluge of advertising in Texas' expensive numerous media markets.   
   Outside/ad spending shows landscape is deep and wide   Beyond the press release bluster and public proclamations about which races are competitive and the optimistic nature both parties put on about the money raised in key contests, the money spent tells the true story about where the landscape lies.   From now until Election Day, at least $700 million in advertising reservations are planned, according to AdImpact, and the number is likely to rise in the final sprint. Three-quarters of that is for races that are either toss-ups or some degree of Republican-favored, according to the Cook Political Report.   Since Sept. 28, Republicans have more than quadrupled their ad spending in the Kansas Senate race, tripled the investment in Mississippi's Senate contest and in House seats in Missouri, Arizona, Pennsylvania and Kentucky.   At the same time, the party has also removed spending from Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia and onetime toss-up House seats in Iowa, Ohio and Nebraska that now favor Democrats.   Democrats have launched a full-court press on the Senate side with millions of dollars in additional ad spending in the existing competitive races in Ohio, Michigan, Maine, Texas and Alaska, while adding Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi and South Carolina to the mix. On the House side, many of the "Red to Blue" and "Districts In Play" designations have been followed by actual spending, like AR-02, MN-01, MT-01 and KY-06.   
   Oct. 15 marked the last major quarterly campaign finance deadline, but large campaign contributions and outside expenditures will be reported with a one- or two-day turnaround all the way through Election Day.

title: Between the coasts, populist Democrats see room to reclaim lost ground in red states
description: Sam Forstag poses for a portrait on a ra
body:
Sam Forstag poses for a portrait on a ranch outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026. A former U.S. Forest Service smokejumper, Forstag is trying to flip a House seat in the state's 1st congressional district.
                
                    Tailyr Irvine for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tailyr Irvine for NPR
    

   
   WESTERN MONTANA — Voters are angry, and an unconventional crop of Democratic candidates see an opening in this year's midterms to reclaim territory others in the party have given up on.   From the Great Plains and Upper Midwest to the Deep South, campaigns are taking a page from a progressive brand of economic populism that once flourished away from the coasts.   They are betting that harnessing anger at corporate power and both parties might succeed when many voters believe the economy and government are not working for working people.   If successful, they could forge a new playbook to compete again in places Democrats used to win.   
   In Montana, former U.S. Forest Service smokejumper Sam Forstag is trying to flip a House seat by speaking directly and from his own experience about the economic stress facing many Montana voters.   
   "I was making 19 bucks an hour jumping out of airplanes for the federal government in a community where you'd be lucky to find a home for a half million bucks," says Forstag, who in 2022 joined an elite team of wildland firefighters parachuting into remote areas. "If a smokejumper is being left behind, a whole lot of other people are being left behind by both political parties."   When President Trump cut nearly 400 Forest Service jobs in Montana last year, Forstag was his union's vice president. Forstag says he tried to reach his Republican congressman, Ryan Zinke.   "Time and time again, I got crickets, so I decided if he's going to come after my coworkers and our members' jobs, I'm going to come and take his," Forstag told a crowd of smokejumpers and wildland firefighters this month at the Great Burn Brewery in Missoula.   Zinke ultimately retired, opening a district that runs some 400 miles between Yellowstone and Glacier National Parks. Trump won the district by double digits in 2024. Now it is considered a toss-up.   
   A mix of factors are upending the typical political dynamics inside the district.   With an influx of wealthy transplants since the pandemic, the Montana housing market has become among the most unaffordable in the nation. That squeeze has been compounded as the cost of groceries, gas and health insurance have also soared.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Former Montana Senator Jon Tester on his ranch in Big Sandy, Montana on October 6, 2026. Tester says the Democratic brand is not good in Montana, but believes the Iran war and rising costs could prompt some voters to give his party another look.
                
                    Tailyr Irvine for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tailyr Irvine for NPR
    

   
   How the Democratic brand tarnished   Montana has not usually been thought of as a swing state in recent years. Not long ago, voters here regularly elected Republicans and Democrats. But as the urge for disruption and a strain of populist rhetoric trained on cultural elites and immigrants helped propel Trump to victory in 2016, Democrats increasingly struggled to hang on.   Sandi Ramos voted for President Obama twice before backing President Trump. Still she continued voting for Montana's Democratic senator, Jon Tester.   In the Biden era, Ramos soured on Democrats more broadly. She says overall she is pleased with the job Trump is doing, despite not liking him personally, and says it would be hard to vote for a Democrat, even Forstag.   "I don't think anything could happen that fast to make me vote for him," Ramos says. "Although I really respect him as a person and I like him."   
   With support from split ticket voters like Ramos, Tester was able to outperform national Democrats for years. But that record of electoral success came to an end in 2024, when he lost his bid for reelection.    Following the Blackfoot River and then crossing the Continental Divide, golden aspen trees give way to wide-open fields for wheat and peas where Tester's family has farmed for over a century.   "Where you're standing right now in 1960 was pretty damn blue," Tester says. "These were the children of homesteaders in the Great Depression. They understand the role government played. Before my grandfather died, he said if it wasn't for FDR, we wouldn't be on this place."   
   Tester says the Democratic brand here is not good. He believes many national Democrats have written off places between the Appalachians and the Rockies. But as the Iran war and tariffs spike prices for fertilizer and fuel under Trump, Tester says some voters may be willing to give Democrats another look.   'Changing whose in those damn rooms'    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sam Forstag hears from farmers and ranchers at an event on a ranch outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026.
                
                    Tailyr Irvine for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tailyr Irvine for NPR
    

   
   That is one reason Forstag spent a sunny Wednesday afternoon talking with a group of farmers and ranchers gathered at Peterson Angus Ranch. Proprietor Sue Peterson also chairs the small Granite County Democratic Party. Atop a bluff with vistas in all directions, she says she has one theory why Democrats sometimes struggle to connect with ranchers or farmers in places they used to win.   "If you're dealing with animals, you're dealing with life and death all the time and sometimes the decisions are hard and it's hard to relate to someone in a suit," Peterson says.   Forstag says it is frustrating to hear so many Democrats talk about affordability like a novel messaging strategy or a buzzword.   "We don't change this by giving a new term to it," Forstag says in an interview. "We change it by changing who's in those damn rooms. Because there are politicians who have been sitting in those offices for 10, 20, 30 years and nothing has changed."   For Forstag, running as a populist means recalibrating the relationship between the people in power in Washington and the regular people who send them there.   "I'm going to answer to the people I've worked with for the last eight years," Forstag says. "I'm going to answer to people like the kid I was growing up, whose belly is full because of food stamps. It does not feel like that's who Congress is answering to right now."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
                Forstag poses for a portrait outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026. He says it is frustrating to hear Democrats talk about affordability like it is a buzzword. "We don't change this by giving a new term to it," he says.
                
                    Tailyr Irvine for NPR
                
                hide caption
    
        Tailyr Irvine for NPR
    

   
   Prairie populism is having a moment   With a campaign hyper-focused on answering the economic pain shaping the lives of voters, Forstag has managed to attract endorsements from the party's left flank, like New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and also more moderate members of the Blue Dog Caucus in the House.   
   "Populist language is a way to unify disparate groups who might lean towards or be willing to vote for Democrats, but might have problems with the beliefs or the priorities of one or another constituency within the Democratic Party," says Georgetown University professor Michael Kazin, who studies the history of American populism.   In places like Iowa, Arkansas and Wisconsin this year, candidates are embracing a more specific identity – as prairie populists, a nod to the late 19th century political movement with Great Plains roots that united small farmers and workers against corporate monopolies.   Kazin says it was also a reaction to states in the heartland feeling neglected in favor of more populous, urban states on the coasts. Kazin says claiming this identity today allows candidates to tap into the anger that's fueling anti-establishment campaigns across the country this year, without alienating voters in more conservative-leaning states who might be put off by the party's toxic brand or divisive social issues.   
   In Iowa, Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek calls himself a "common sense prairie populist" and says his north star is "to go up there and fight for the people that can't afford to make a political donation or afford a lobbyist."   The Democratic candidate for governor, Rob Sand, is campaigning on issues like the big agriculture corporations stymieing politicians from addressing polluted water supplies.   In Kansas, Democrats have nominated the Rev. Adam Hamilton as their candidate for Senate. Hamilton does not use the kind of anti-establishment rhetoric employed by other Democrats showing traction in red states. But he often ends his stump speech citing the Wizard of Oz, which some historians see as an allegory for the 19th century populist movement.    "Do you remember what the scarecrow needed? A brain. And then what did the Tin Man need? The heart. And what did the Cowardly Lion need? Courage," Hamilton tells crowds. "This is what's missing in the United States Senate right now."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Forstag hears from farmers and ranchers at an event on a ranch outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026.
                
                    Tailyr Irvine for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tailyr Irvine for NPR
    

   
   For some Democrats, embracing this ethos is less about a position on the ideological spectrum and more about speaking to voters fed up with the status quo.   
   "The most common thing I've heard, whether I'm in Kansas or Wisconsin or Michigan, is we want a new generation of leaders and we want big and bold ideas. People are absolutely done with what they've known in the past," Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin told NPR after stumping for progressive Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a local Democratic club this summer in Michigan.   
   Jane Kleeb, the state party chair in Nebraska where Democrats are backing a mechanic running as an independent and a populist for Senate, says it is perplexing when Democrats complain that the only way to win power in the Senate is to reform its structure. She says the answer is to earnestly compete in more states.   "So trying to focus on eight battlegrounds never made mathematical sense," says Kleeb, who is also a vice chair at the Democratic National Committee.   With frustrated voters, candidates see an opening   But if Democrats gain ground in Republican-leaning places, it might not be clear how much of that success is a reflection on the type of candidates and messages or just the deteriorating national environment for Republicans.   GOP candidates are also feeling the pressure to speak to anger over the economy.   Campaigning across the vast district in an RV, Forstag's Republican opponent, veteran Aaron Flint, is promising to "make the Montana dream affordable again." As a conservative radio host, Flint has an intimate relationship with many Montana voters and hears about the challenges they are dealing with.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Aaron Flint, the GOP candidate for the House in Montana's 1st District, speaks ahead of an address by President Trump in Kalispell, Mont. on Oct. 14.
                
                    Ross D. Franklin/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ross D. Franklin/AP
    

   
   He is also trying to pierce Forstag's working class biography and effort to appeal to the middle, pointing out Forstag has campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and lobbied in the off seasons for the ACLU. Flint says if Democrats take power, they will hike taxes and make Montana's problems worse.   "I'm not just running because of deep frustration with the damage that was done to this party by the Democrat party," Flint said in an interview after a stop in the old mining town of Butte. "I'm also running because there's some Republicans back in Washington that aren't doing enough to fix everything either."   
   Voter Nicholas Babcock is skeptical. He is a mail carrier in nearby Anaconda, where an old smelter for the once behemoth Anaconda Copper Company rises 585 feet above town. Babcock voted for Trump three times. He says the first term was more good than bad.   "The second term is the exact opposite," he says. "We have seen a complete betrayal of almost every campaign promise that was made. It just feels almost like a slap in the face that we were sold one thing and none of it was delivered."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sam Forstag speaks at a rally geared toward former and current firefighters at the Great Burn Brewery on October 5, 2026 in Missoula, Montana.

   So Babcock showed up at a Forstag town hall. He says his hero was Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist who was assassinated last year. "He would listen to absolutely anybody, discuss anything with anybody," Babcock says. "I'm absolutely willing to change my mind."   Babcock says Forstag also knows what it's like to punch a clock and thinks he might actually buck the establishment. He hopes this politician will follow through.   With reporting by Barbara Sprunt in Nebraska, Stephen Fowler in Kansas and Danielle Kurtzleben in Iowa.

schema.headline: Between the coasts, populist Democrats see room to reclaim lost ground in red states
